description: Lightweight technique registry. Rows do not require Landscape/Shortlist/Ingest/Normalization. Fill: docs/practices/PRACTICE_LIBRARY_FILL_V1.md

techniques.note: Equal-count / four-phase hold research became a sunk-cost trap. Do not continue Safety Review V1.1 or targeted safety work on this type. Use another suitable type for the need. Existing library items stay provisional without technique_id.

techniques.canonical_description: A short unforced breath cycle: inhale gently through the nose, then exhale longer than the inhale, without a hold. Counting (for example two in / three out, or five in / seven out) is only a pace aid. Breath-holds are not part of this product version.

source_refs.source: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS — Breathing pattern disorders and physiotherapy
source_refs.locus: Breathing control exercises, Step 2 Slow breathing (in for one-to-two-or-three, out for one-to-three-or-four; out-breath passive); during activity, out-breath longer than in-breath
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation only. Not imported as a breathlessness-retraining protocol. Optional post-exhale pause in that page is not in this product version.

source_refs.source: Berkshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust — How breathing can reduce stress and anxiety
source_refs.locus: Tip 1: rectangular breathing, inhale 5 seconds and exhale 7 seconds, then repeating
source_refs.note: official_health. Longer out-breath, no hold in this example.

safety_notes: Do not force the out-breath or take bigger breaths.
Stop if dizzy or faint.
This product version has no breath-hold.

techniques.canonical_description: Sit with one chosen object of attention: a visual point, the breath, a sound, or a short phrase. Keep attention there. When the mind wanders, notice it and return. Wandering is part of the method. This product version is not a clinical mindfulness protocol and does not use breath-holds.

source_refs.source: NCCIH — Meditation and Mindfulness: Effectiveness and Safety
source_refs.locus: What are meditation and mindfulness?: some types maintain mental focus on a particular sensation such as breathing, a sound, a visual image, or a mantra
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation. Efficacy claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic — Meditation: A simple, fast way to reduce stress
source_refs.locus: Parts of meditation / Focused attention: focus on an object, image, mantra, or breathing; when the mind wanders, slowly return
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation. Benefit lists and illness claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Harvard Health — Mindfulness practice for focus
source_refs.locus: Focused attention (FA) meditation: keep attention on a particular object or sensation; if the mind wanders, return to the focal point
source_refs.note: academic_description. Method confirmation. Productivity/efficacy claims not imported.

safety_notes: Stop if the practice makes you feel worse or more agitated.
Not a treatment for attention or mental-health conditions.

techniques.note: The LLM probe (gentle shorter mouth exhale) is not a confirmed method. Real activating-breath techniques are forceful/pumping (bhastrika, kapalabhati, firebreath): no single safe product kernel, material safety. Do not map this type onto pranayama to save the preferred slot. Use another suitable type for the need.

techniques.canonical_description: A short unforced movement of a few joints, seated or standing: for example circle the wrists, then the shoulders, within a comfortable range. Stop if it hurts. This product version is not a stretch-hold protocol, not a workout, and not a treatment.

source_refs.source: NHS — Sitting exercises
source_refs.locus: Gentle sitting exercises to improve mobility; move as far as is comfortable; examples include hip marching and joint/neck movement, not a gym workout
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation. Exercise-prescription counts, clot/disease claims, and named stretch scripts not imported.

source_refs.source: NHS — Why we should sit less
source_refs.locus: UK Chief Medical Officers' Physical Activity Guidelines: break up long periods of sitting with at least light activity
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for brief light movement. Illness/sitting-risk claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Chartered Society of Physiotherapy — Desk-based exercises
source_refs.locus: Break up prolonged sitting with short bursts of activity; keep moving; stretches should not cause pain or tingling
source_refs.note: professional_body. Method confirmation. Named stretch-hold scripts and wall-press sets not imported.

safety_notes: Stay in a comfortable range. Stop if it hurts.
Not a treatment and not an exercise prescription.

techniques.canonical_description: Briefly notice what is available to the senses in the present surroundings: name something you see, something you hear, something you touch. Do not explain. Count schemes such as 5-4-3-2-1 or 3-2-1 are pace aids, not the kernel. This product version is not a panic, trauma, or dissociation protocol.

source_refs.source: Oxford Health NHS CAMHS — Ground yourself
source_refs.locus: Grounding: move attention to the present, the current environment, and the feel of being in that place; notice small sensory details; 5-4-3-2-1 is one way
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation. Anxiety/sleep-treatment claims and the named 5-4-3-2-1 script not imported.

source_refs.source: NHS inform — Grounding exercises
source_refs.locus: Grounding as a technique to take the mind off uncomfortable symptoms or thoughts; 5,4,3,2,1 listed as one exercise among others
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation. Symptom-reduction claims and the counted script not imported.

safety_notes: Stop if the practice makes you feel worse.
Not a treatment for anxiety, panic, trauma, or dissociation.

techniques.canonical_description: Answer one specific question in your own words, briefly. A conclusion, lesson, or decision is not required. Spelling and length are not part of the method. Structured writing protocols (CBT thought records, Gibbs/Rolfe professional reflection, timed expressive writing) are not this product version.

source_refs.source: Best For You — Journalling for mental health (NHS-clinician approved)
source_refs.locus: Journal prompts: some are just one question or a title; others are more structured or linked to a therapy approach such as CBT; writing is for you, spelling and grammar do not matter
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation. Benefit lists, thought-record templates, and therapy claims not imported.

source_refs.source: VCU Writing Center — Reflective writing
source_refs.locus: Reflection is a personal response to a prompt; there is no right or wrong way to respond; start from the prompt
source_refs.note: academic_description. Method confirmation. Essay templates and learning-outcome claims not imported.

safety_notes: Stop if writing makes you feel worse.
Not a treatment and not a CBT thought record.

techniques.canonical_description: A short, realistic statement that names the present challenge and affirms the person's existing capacity to cope with it, based on lived experience or current resources. The statement is specific, believable, and phrased in the first person. It is not a prediction of success, a wish, or a guarantee of outcome. It is spoken once or a few times, then the person returns to the situation.

source_refs.source: College of Cognitive Behavioural Therapies — Rational coping statements: more than just 'live, laugh, love'
source_refs.locus: Rational coping statements are short, specific, reality-based phrases that challenge negative thoughts by acknowledging the difficulty of a situation and affirming the capacity to cope; example: 'I have handled difficult situations before, and I can handle this one too'
source_refs.note: clinical_psychology. Method confirmation. CBT/REBT model. Efficacy and treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: NHS inform — Anxiety self-help guide
source_refs.locus: CBT-based guide: reducing avoidance by continuing to confront situations helps prove to yourself that you can manage them; self-help techniques are tools, not a replacement for professional support if needed
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for realistic self-efficacy statements and behavioral management of anxiety. Diagnosis/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Stop if the statement makes you feel worse or increases self-criticism.
Not a treatment for anxiety, depression, or any mental-health condition.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief somatic exercise in which the person intentionally tenses a small, high-tension area of the body (shoulders lifted toward the ears), holds the tension for a few seconds, and then releases it, noticing the contrast between the tight and relaxed state. It is an abbreviated, single-area form of progressive muscle relaxation used to become aware of physical tension and to let it drop. It does not require a full-body sequence or a particular posture.

source_refs.source: NHS inform — Progressive muscle relaxation
source_refs.locus: Tense and relax muscles one area at a time; list includes shoulders. Hold tension for a few seconds, release, let the muscle relax. Useful for reducing tension and becoming aware of early signs of anger or panic.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for abbreviated single-area tension-release. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic — Relaxation techniques: Try these steps to lower stress
source_refs.locus: Progressive muscle relaxation: tense muscles for about five seconds and then relax for 30 seconds, repeating; focus on the difference between tension and relaxation.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for tension-release contrast. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: StatPearls — Relaxation Techniques (NCBI Bookshelf)
source_refs.locus: Progressive Muscle Relaxation involves tensing and releasing muscles, focusing on the alleviation of tension and the experience of relaxation; targets the symptom of tension associated with anxiety.
source_refs.note: medical_literature. Method confirmation for tensing/releasing muscle groups to contrast tension and relaxation. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Stop if the movement causes pain or sharp discomfort; do not force the shoulders upward.
Not a treatment for anxiety, chronic pain, or any medical condition.

techniques.canonical_description: A short, seated body-focused relaxation in which the person rests attention on a simple physical sensation (heaviness in the hands or arms) and links it to the out-breath. It is a brief fragment of systematic focusing or body-scan relaxation, not a full progressive muscle-relaxation sequence. The aim is to notice tension and allow the body to soften for a few breaths, then return to the situation.

source_refs.source: CUH NHS — Systematic focusing: relaxation technique
source_refs.locus: Get comfortable; focus on breathing; guide attention through body areas; aim for a soft, heavy feeling in the muscles; shoulders, arms, and hands become limp and heavy; tension is eased using the mind, not movement.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for brief body-focused relaxation using heaviness as a relaxation signal. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic — Relaxation techniques: Try these steps to lower stress
source_refs.locus: Relaxation techniques include meditation, deep breathing, and autogenic training; person focuses on relaxing breathing or physical sensations, such as relaxing each arm or leg one by one; done in a quiet spot with eyes closed if comfortable.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for meditation/body-focused relaxation and attention to physical sensations. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: NHS inform — Progressive muscle relaxation
source_refs.locus: Tense and relax one area at a time, then focus on each body part and allow remaining tension to release on the out-breath; includes shoulders, arms, hands, and face.
source_refs.note: official_health. Context for releasing tension with breath and body attention; the item is a non-tensing fragment. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Stop if focusing on the body increases anxiety or dizziness.
Not a treatment for anxiety, insomnia, or any medical condition.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief pre-sleep meditation in which the person lies down, closes the eyes, and directs attention to one small area of physical tension (for example the jaw) while breathing out slowly. The goal is to wind down and signal readiness for sleep, not to force sleep or perform a full body scan. It is used as a short, repeatable part of a relaxing bedtime routine.

source_refs.source: NHS inform — Sleep hygiene
source_refs.locus: Spend time winding down before bedtime; while meditation and mindfulness is not for everyone, find a way to relax that gives a sense of peace and calm; some people find a bath or shower before bed helps.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for wind-down / relaxation as part of sleep preparation. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic Health System — 5 ways to get better sleep
source_refs.locus: Adults sleep better with a bedtime routine; do the same thing before bed each night to prepare the body for rest; stick to activities that promote relaxation, such as gentle stretching, reading, or meditation.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for a bedtime relaxation routine. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: NHS inform — Insomnia
source_refs.locus: Improve sleep hygiene by creating a relaxing bedtime routine; if you can't sleep, get up and do a relaxing activity, then return when sleepy.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for relaxing activity before/during sleep attempts. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for insomnia or any sleep disorder.
If sleep problems persist, consult a healthcare professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A short-period behavioral rule in which the person chooses a fixed latest bedtime and commits to lying down by that time for a set number of consecutive days. The rule is about schedule consistency, not about forcing sleep, changing sleep duration, or managing insomnia. It is a lightweight, self-administered discipline rather than a full sleep-hygiene or CBT-I protocol.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic — Sleep tips: 6 steps to better sleep
source_refs.locus: Stick to a sleep schedule: go to bed and get up at the same time every day, including weekends; being consistent reinforces the body's sleep-wake cycle.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for fixed bedtime consistency as a sleep discipline. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic — Insomnia treatment: Cognitive behavioral therapy instead of sleeping pills
source_refs.locus: CBT-I includes changing routine: set a consistent bedtime and wake time; avoid naps; use the bed only for sleep and sex; if unable to fall asleep within 20 minutes, leave the bedroom and return when sleepy while maintaining the wake-up time.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for consistent sleep schedule as a behavioral rule. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: NHS inform — Sleep hygiene
source_refs.locus: Regular sleep routine: go to bed and wake up at the same time every day; spend time winding down before bedtime; consistent habits improve the sleep routine.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for regular bedtime routine. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for insomnia or any sleep disorder.
If sleep problems persist, consult a healthcare professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief behavioral-activation exercise in which the person names one concrete action that can be completed in about two minutes and does it immediately, then stops. The action is smaller than the task it is attached to and is chosen to break the inertia of stuckness or low energy without requiring motivation, planning, or a larger commitment. It is a single-step fragment, not a full activity schedule or CBT protocol.

source_refs.source: NHS East London Foundation Trust (ELFT) — Behavioural Activation
source_refs.locus: Behavioural activation works by re-engaging with activities despite low mood; start with small, achievable, specific activities; plan what, when, where, and who; graded approach from easier to harder tasks.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for starting with a small, specific, achievable activity when motivation is low. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic Anxiety Coach — Depression Treatment Behavioral Activation
source_refs.locus: Break the cycle of inactivity and low mood by slowly doing more important or enjoyable activities; mood and energy improve as activity increases; activities include mastery, social, and healthy-habit categories.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for re-engaging with a small activity despite low energy/mood. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Psychology Tools — How To Use Behavioral Activation To Overcome Depression
source_refs.locus: Increase activity even if you do not feel like it; break activities down into smaller steps; start with low-difficulty activities; plan specific what/when/where/who details.
source_refs.note: professional_education. Method confirmation for small-step activation and immediate low-difficulty action. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for depression or any mental health condition.
If low mood or lack of motivation persists, consult a healthcare professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief self-check-in practice in which the person names one word for what they are feeling right now, notices one place in the body where that feeling lives, and stops. No explanation, no story, no attempt to fix or deepen the emotion. The practice is a momentary emotional-awareness and affect-labeling gesture, not a therapeutic exercise or diagnostic tool.

source_refs.source: Greater Good Science Center — Naming Your Emotions
source_refs.locus: Naming an emotion can dampen the amygdala alarm response and reduce the severity of the emotional response in the moment; observe body and mind, name the feeling, do not hold it in or judge it.
source_refs.note: public_education. Method confirmation for a brief pause-name-body-noticing practice. Efficacy claims limited to momentary down-regulation of strong negative emotion.

source_refs.source: NHS Lothian — Emotion Workbook
source_refs.locus: Recognising and naming the emotion; noticing where it is felt in the body; saying the word out loud or writing it down; asking what else is felt.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for recognising, naming, and locating an emotion in the body. Not imported as a treatment protocol.

source_refs.source: Torre & Lieberman (2018) — Putting feelings into words: affect labeling as implicit emotion regulation
source_refs.locus: Affect labeling (putting feelings into words) can reduce self-reported distress and amygdala response to aversive stimuli; effects correlate with reappraisal benefits.
source_refs.note: academic_review. Mechanism support for labeling reducing emotional intensity in high-arousal aversive contexts. Not a universal or long-term effect claim.

source_refs.source: Nook et al. (2022) — Affect labeling: the role of timing and intensity (PLOS ONE)
source_refs.locus: Affect labeling reduced distress in high-intensity aversive conditions but increased distress in low-intensity conditions; use with caution and stop if it worsens feeling.
source_refs.note: academic_study. Safety boundary: do not present affect labeling as always helpful; it can backfire in low-intensity states.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for anxiety, depression, trauma, or any mental health condition.
If the feeling is overwhelming or worsens during the practice, stop and seek professional support.
Do not use this practice to process trauma or persistent emotional crises without a qualified professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief private-writing practice in which the person writes a few short sentences from their own perspective without editing or revising. The aim is to put current thoughts or feelings into words as a moment of self-connection, not to analyse, solve, or process a difficult experience. It is a single, short fragment rather than a multi-day expressive-writing protocol or therapeutic intervention.

source_refs.source: NHS Lanarkshire — Writing for Wellbeing
source_refs.locus: Writing helps explore emotions, good and bad, and gain a better understanding of our own feelings; reflective writing is a place to express yourself, your thoughts, feelings and ideas; leave a notebook anywhere for a spare minute.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for brief private writing as a self-expression / self-connection practice. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Cambridge University Hospitals NHS — Write Your Self
source_refs.locus: A resource to explore creative writing and encourage self-expression; includes journaling, expressive writing, reminiscence, and self-reflection activities.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for journaling and self-expression writing. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Greater Good Science Center — Expressive Writing
source_refs.locus: Write freely about your feelings and thoughts for an experience of hurt; try not to edit or judge what you write; your writing is for your eyes only and for your own well-being.
source_refs.note: public_education. Method confirmation for private, unedited writing as a self-expression practice. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for any mental health condition.
If writing brings up overwhelming feelings, stop and consider speaking with a healthcare professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief behavioral practice in which the person initiates one small, concrete act of connection with another person (for example, one short message, one honest question, or one brief check-in) and stops after that single step. The action is chosen to be small enough to complete without relying on mood or reciprocity, and is not a conversation script, relationship repair protocol, or social-skills training.

source_refs.source: NHS Essex ICB — Looking after your mental health
source_refs.locus: Start small; choose one realistic action such as speaking to someone you trust; boost mood through connection and routine; if symptoms persist, seek support.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for a small, single social-connection action as part of self-care. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Liu et al. (2025) — Behavioral activation for social connection: A systematic review (Journal of Social and Personal Relationships)
source_refs.locus: Behavioral activation improves functional dimensions of social connection (loneliness, perceived support) by increasing small, structured social actions; strongest effects when delivered with coaching and scheduled.
source_refs.note: academic_review. Mechanism support for small, scheduled social actions improving perceived connection. Not a claim that a single action cures loneliness.

source_refs.source: Laidlaw et al. (2020) — Improving Social Connectedness for Homebound Older Adults (PubMed)
source_refs.locus: Tele-delivered behavioral activation increased social interaction and satisfaction with social support and decreased loneliness compared to friendly visits alone.
source_refs.note: academic_study. Support for structured small social interactions increasing connectedness outcomes. Not a universal or self-administered claim.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for social anxiety, loneliness disorder, or any mental health condition.
If the only available relationships are unsafe or harmful, choose a different action or speak with a professional.
If feelings of loneliness or disconnection persist, seek support from a healthcare professional or trusted service.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief micro-creativity practice in which the person makes one tiny, low-stakes mark or gesture (for example, one line, one shape, one word) and stops without editing or judging the result. The aim is to shift attention away from rumination or stuckness onto a simple, immediate act of creation; it is not an art exercise, a skill-building session, or a creative-arts therapy protocol.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic Press — The intersection of art and health: How art can help promote well-being
source_refs.locus: Creating visual art like drawings or paintings can provide enjoyment and distraction from pain and anxiety; artistic expression and appreciation can benefit physical and mental well-being; the process of creating can support well-being without requiring professional art skills.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for a brief, low-stakes act of creating visual art as a well-being practice. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic — Stress relievers: Tips to tame stress
source_refs.locus: If music is not your interest, turn attention to another hobby such as gardening, sewing, reading, or sketching; choose anything that makes you focus on what you are doing rather than what you think you should be doing.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for a brief, focused creative action (sketching) as a distraction/stress-relief practice. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust — Arts for Good Health
source_refs.locus: Being creative is good for mental health; Arts for Good Health courses are short, accessible, require no previous experience, and use creativity to boost health and wellbeing.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for short, accessible creative activities supporting mental wellbeing. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for anxiety, depression, or any mental health condition.
If the practice brings up strong self-criticism or distress, stop and consider speaking with a healthcare professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief decision-making practice in which the person names one single task or priority that is most important right now and deliberately sets the rest aside. The aim is to reduce overwhelm and attention fragmentation by committing to one next step rather than creating a full plan or to-do list; it is not a productivity system, time-blocking method, or problem-solving protocol.

source_refs.source: NHS England — The expectations of line managers in relation to people management
source_refs.locus: Managers should set direction for individuals and teams; people need to be clear about what is expected of them and what their priorities should be; setting a clear direction helps enable people to deliver effectively and manage workload more effectively.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for clarifying one priority to manage workload and focus. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: NHS Elect — Time Management & Productivity Programme
source_refs.locus: Evaluate competing demands using structured prioritisation frameworks such as urgent versus important and impact versus effort; make better decisions about what deserves your time and translate those decisions into a clear and manageable plan.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for picking one priority from competing demands using simple prioritisation frameworks. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic Research — Mindful Breathing: Roberto P. Benzo, M.D.
source_refs.locus: When you do these exercises, have the sole intention to feel your body moving; just that. Single tasking. One thing. Pick a specific place and time to practice every day.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine/research. Method confirmation for committing to a single, specific task or intention at a time. Treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for anxiety, ADHD, or any mental health condition.
If choosing one priority feels impossible due to overwhelming demands, consider speaking with a manager, healthcare professional, or trusted support person.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief transition practice that marks the boundary between two activities by cognitively closing the previous task, making a simple physical movement, and opening attention to the next task. The aim is to reduce attention residue and task-set inertia when switching contexts; it is not a rest break, a productivity planning session, or a task-completion ritual.

source_refs.source: Leroy, S. (2009). Why is it so hard to do my work? The challenge of attention residue when switching between work tasks. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 109(2), 168-181
source_refs.locus: Unfinished tasks leave attention residue that impairs performance on subsequent tasks; completing or cognitively closing the prior task before switching reduces this residue and helps attention move fully to the next task.
source_refs.note: academic. Method confirmation for a brief closure-and-switch practice between tasks. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Leroy, S., & Glomb, T. M. (2018). Tasks Interrupted: How Anticipating Time Pressure on Resumption of an Interrupted Task Causes Attention Residue and Low Performance on Interrupting Tasks and How a 'Ready-to-Resume' Plan Mitigates the Effects. Organization Science, 29(3), 380-397
source_refs.locus: A brief ready-to-resume plan that documents where one stopped and what to do next reduces attention residue and improves performance on the interrupting task by creating cognitive closure.
source_refs.note: academic. Method confirmation for a short, structured transition plan that closes one task before moving to the next. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: NHS Every Mind Matters — 6 tips to tackle working from home
source_refs.locus: Making time for breaks and setting a boundary to stop work at the end of the day help manage stress and maintain focus; regular short breaks help you feel more focused when you return.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for a brief pause and boundary between work periods. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for ADHD, anxiety, or any neurological or mental health condition.
If difficulty switching attention is persistent, severe, or accompanied by distress, consider speaking with a healthcare professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A brief somatic recovery practice in which the person deliberately tenses a small muscle group (for example, fists, shoulders, or jaw) while inhaling, then releases the tension while exhaling for a few repetitions. The aim is to use the contrast between tension and release to reduce bodily tension and support recovery; it is not a full-body progressive muscle relaxation protocol, a treatment for anxiety or pain, or a sleep induction technique.

source_refs.source: NHS inform — Progressive muscle relaxation
source_refs.locus: Progressive muscle relaxation involves tensing and relaxing the muscles one area at a time; take a breath in and tense the muscles in one area, hold for a few seconds, breathe out and release the tension, let the muscles relax; repeat in different parts of the body; if an area is painful, miss it out.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for a brief, localized tense-and-release practice. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Mayo Clinic — Relaxation techniques: Try these steps to lower stress
source_refs.locus: Progressive muscle relaxation: focus on slowly tensing and then relaxing each muscle group; tense muscles for about five seconds and then relax for 30 seconds, and repeat; can be done in a quiet area without interruptions.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for a short, repeated tense-and-release cycle. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs — Whole Health Library: Progressive Muscle Relaxation
source_refs.locus: PMR is a two-step relaxation practice: create tension in a specific muscle group and notice what tension feels like, then release the tension and notice what a relaxed muscle feels like; hold tension for five seconds while breathing in, then release and relax all at once; do not strain or overly tense the muscle, and skip a body part if it causes discomfort.
source_refs.note: government_health. Method confirmation for a small, repeated tense-and-release practice. Treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for anxiety, chronic pain, insomnia, or any medical or mental health condition.
Do not tense to the point of pain or cramping; if a muscle group is injured or painful, skip it.
If persistent tension, pain, or distress occurs, stop and consider speaking with a healthcare professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A short-period commitment rule in which the person chooses one small, specific action and commits to performing it at the same time or after the same daily cue for a set number of consecutive days (for example, seven days). The aim is to create a stable context for repeated practice and reduce daily decision-making; it is not a guarantee of habit formation, a long-term behaviour-change programme, or a treatment for motivation or attention difficulties.

source_refs.source: NICE — Behaviour change: individual approaches (PH49), Recommendation 10
source_refs.locus: Help people to develop routines that support the new behaviour; note that small, manageable changes to daily routine are most likely to be maintained; ensure behaviour change is maintained for at least a year.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for small, manageable routine changes as a behaviour-change support. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Lally & Gardner (2012) — Making health habitual: the psychology of ‘habit-formation’ and general practice, British Journal of General Practice
source_refs.locus: Advice for creating habits: repeat a chosen behaviour in the same context until it becomes automatic and effortless; the context can be an event or a time of day; a cue within an existing daily routine provides a convenient and stable starting point; patients should choose the target behaviour themselves and add a new behaviour rather than focus on stopping an existing one.
source_refs.note: academic. Method confirmation for a self-selected, repeated action anchored to a stable daily cue. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Keller et al. (2021) — Habit formation following routine-based versus time-based cue planning: A randomized controlled trial, British Journal of Health Psychology
source_refs.locus: Linking a behaviour to a daily routine or a specific time was similarly effective for habit formation; interventions should encourage persons to repeatedly carry out their planned behaviour in response to the planned cue; plan enactment was a key predictor for automaticity.
source_refs.note: academic. Method confirmation for repeated enactment of a behaviour tied to a planned cue (time or routine). Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for ADHD, executive dysfunction, procrastination, or any mental health condition.
A short consecutive streak does not guarantee automaticity or long-term habit formation; habits typically take longer and vary widely between individuals.

If the chosen action becomes painful, unsafe, or impossible to sustain, stop or revise it; if persistent difficulty with routine or self-regulation occurs, consider speaking with a healthcare professional.

techniques.canonical_description: A short-period discipline rule in which the person reduces attention-drawing inputs by keeping only one information stream or task open at a time and closing or disabling extra ones immediately. The aim is to lower task-switching and environmental distraction by simplifying the attention space; it is not a treatment for ADHD or any attention disorder, a productivity system, or a guarantee of focus.

source_refs.source: American Psychological Association — Multitasking: Switching costs
source_refs.locus: Multitasking creates switching costs: repeatedly shifting between tasks can take more time and involve more error; understanding these costs can help people choose strategies that boost efficiency by avoiding multitasking, especially with complex tasks.
source_refs.note: research/official_psychology. Method confirmation for reducing open tasks/inputs to limit switching costs. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Harvard Health Publishing — The art of monotasking
source_refs.locus: Monotasking means focusing on only one job until it is completed; strategies include blocking distractions, turning off the phone or setting it to do not disturb, and creating a distraction-free environment; even a three-second interruption can double the risk of errors.
source_refs.note: clinical_medicine. Method confirmation for a single-open-input rule and closing distractions. Treatment claims not imported.

source_refs.source: Leeds Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust — Digital Wellbeing: Making your tech work for you
source_refs.locus: Managing notifications using Do Not Disturb, time-blocking email and checking at designated times, and taking breaks away from screens can help reduce digital overwhelm and maintain focus.
source_refs.note: official_health. Method confirmation for limiting digital notifications and reducing open inputs. Efficacy/treatment claims not imported.

safety_notes: Not a treatment for ADHD, executive dysfunction, or any attention or neurological condition.
If persistent difficulty concentrating, impulsivity, or distress is present, consider speaking with a healthcare professional.
This rule is an environmental simplification; it does not guarantee focus or eliminate internal distractions.
